issues.legal_issue: Whether profit from an isolated purchase and resale of property is taxable as business income when the transaction is not connected with the assessee’s existing business.
material_facts: The assessee carried on a business dealing in iron scrap and hardware, but had never carried on a jute-pressing business.

The assessee purchased a jute press and appurtenant property subject to pending litigation, repaired the factory and kept it in working condition, but did not organize or begin a jute-pressing business.
The assessee agreed to resell the property after receiving an offer soon after the purchase and made a substantial profit.

The property was capable of being let out and had previously been let out; apart from the expectation of profit and its realization, there was no evidence establishing that the purchase was intended as a trading venture.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was not shown to be an adventure in the nature of trade, so the profit was not taxable as business income. The question was answered in the negative and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 10 and 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, business income includes profits from an adventure in the nature of trade. The revenue must establish that the profit falls within the taxing provision. Whether a transaction is such an adventure is a mixed question of law and fact, determined from the collective effect of the circumstances; no single fact is decisive. A transaction related to the assessee’s usual business, or dealings such as subdividing, altering, treating, or converting an acquired commodity before resale, may support an inference of trade. But profit motive or an expectation of resale at a profit alone does not turn an accretion to capital into taxable income, and a purchase of property cannot, without more, be assumed to be a trading venture. The Court relied on G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Saroj Kumar Mazumdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, West Bengal, and considered the illustrative authorities Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge v. Commissioner of Inland Revenue, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold, and Leeming v. Jones.

rule.if: income_tax_profit_assessment and isolated_asset_transaction and unrelated_to_existing_business and property_not_ordinary_trading_commodity and no_business_operations_on_asset and resale_expectation_only

predicates.income_tax_profit_assessment: The proceeding determines whether profit from the sale of an acquired asset is taxable as income from business.
predicates.isolated_asset_transaction: The assessee made a single purchase and resale rather than conducting a recurring business in the asset.
predicates.unrelated_to_existing_business: The acquired asset and its intended use were unrelated to the business the assessee ordinarily carried on.
predicates.property_not_ordinary_trading_commodity: The acquired asset was property that could not, from its nature alone, be treated as an ordinary trading commodity.
predicates.no_business_operations_on_asset: The assessee did not organize or carry on the business associated with the acquired asset before reselling it.
predicates.resale_expectation_only: The established circumstances showed an expectation of resale for profit, but did not establish an additional trading purpose for the purchase.

issues.definition: When an income-tax assessment concerns profit from an isolated asset sale, and the transaction is unrelated to the assessee’s business, involves property not ordinarily treated as a trading commodity, includes no business operations on the asset, and is supported only by an expectation of resale, the sale profit is not taxable as business income.
